response.text:
## Preliminary reproducibility note

Parts (2), (5), (6), and (7) depend on the particular 50 simulated training points. Since the problem statement does not provide a random seed or the actual simulated data, there is no unique numerical value for the MLEs, the GP surrogate minimizer, the five added points, or the spline minimizer. Below I give a fully reproducible solution using a specified seed. Running the code produces the requested numerical estimates and plots.

I use an isotropic squared-exponential correlation

\[
\operatorname{Corr}\{Z(x),Z(x')\}
=
\exp\{-\theta \|x-x'\|^2\}.
\]

The true Goldstein-Price function has known global minimum

\[
x^\star_{\text{true}}=(0,-1),\qquad y(x^\star_{\text{true}})=3.
\]

---

# (1) Simulate \(n=50\) training points and visualize

Define the function and simulate training data.

```r
goldstein <- function(x1, x2) {
  A <- 1 + (x1 + x2 + 1)^2 *
    (19 - 14*x1 + 3*x1^2 - 14*x2 + 6*x1*x2 + 3*x2^2)
  
  B <- 30 + (2*x1 - 3*x2)^2 *
    (18 - 32*x1 + 12*x1^2 + 48*x2 - 36*x1*x2 + 27*x2^2)
  
  A * B
}

set.seed(2023)

n <- 50
X <- cbind(
  x1 = runif(n, -2, 2),
  x2 = runif(n, -2, 2)
)

y <- goldstein(X[,1], X[,2])

dat <- data.frame(x1 = X[,1], x2 = X[,2], y = y)
head(dat)
```

## (1a) True function versus \(x_1\) at \(x_2=2\)

```r
xg <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 500)

plot(
  xg, goldstein(xg, 2),
  type = "l", lwd = 2,
  xlab = expression(x[1]),
  ylab = expression(y(x[1], 2)),
  main = expression(paste("Goldstein-Price: ", x[2] == 2))
)
```

At \(x_2=2\), the function reduces to

\[
y(x_1,2)
=
\{1+(x_1+3)^2(3x_1^2-2x_1+3)\}
\{30+4(x_1-3)^2(12x_1^2-104x_1+222)\}.
\]

## (1b) True function versus \(x_2\) at \(x_1=-2\)

```r
plot(
  xg, goldstein(-2, xg),
  type = "l", lwd = 2,
  xlab = expression(x[2]),
  ylab = expression(y(-2, x[2])),
  main = expression(paste("Goldstein-Price: ", x[1] == -2))
)
```

At \(x_1=-2\), the function reduces to

\[
y(-2,x_2)
=
\{1+(x_2-1)^2(3x_2^2-26x_2+59)\}
\{30+(3x_2+4)^2(27x_2^2+120x_2+130)\}.
\]

## (1c) 3D plot with training data labelled

Because \(y\) varies over several orders of magnitude, I plot \(\log_{10}(y)\).

```r
library(plotly)

grid <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 80)
Z <- outer(grid, grid, function(a, b) goldstein(a, b))

plot_ly() %>%
  add_surface(
    x = grid,
    y = grid,
    z = log10(Z),
    opacity = 0.65,
    colorscale = "Viridis"
  ) %>%
  add_markers(
    x = dat$x1,
    y = dat$x2,
    z = log10(dat$y),
    text = paste0("point ", 1:n),
    marker = list(color = "red", size = 4)
  ) %>%
  layout(
    scene = list(
      xaxis = list(title = "x1"),
      yaxis = list(title = "x2"),
      zaxis = list(title = "log10(y)")
    ),
    title = "Goldstein-Price surface with 50 training points"
  )
```

---

# (2) GP surrogate and MLEs

We model

\[
Y(x)=\mu+Z(x),
\]

where

\[
Z(\cdot)\sim GP\{0,\sigma^2 R_\theta(\cdot,\cdot)\},
\]

with

\[
R_\theta(x,x')
=
\exp\{-\theta \|x-x'\|^2\}.
\]

Let

\[
R_\theta = \left[
\exp\{-\theta \|x_i-x_j\|^2\}
\right]_{i,j=1}^n.
\]

Then

\[
Y=(Y(x_1),\dots,Y(x_n))^\top
\sim
N_n(\mu \mathbf 1,\sigma^2 R_\theta).
\]

The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\mu,\sigma^2,\theta)
=
-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac n2\log \sigma^2
-\frac 12 \log |R_\theta|
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
(y-\mu \mathbf 1)^\top R_\theta^{-1}(y-\mu \mathbf 1).
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the MLE of \(\mu\) is the generalized least-squares estimator

\[
\widehat \mu(\theta)
=
\frac{\mathbf 1^\top R_\theta^{-1}y}
{\mathbf 1^\top R_\theta^{-1}\mathbf 1}.
\]

The MLE of \(\sigma^2\) is

\[
\widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
=
\frac{1}{n}
(y-\widehat\mu(\theta)\mathbf 1)^\top
R_\theta^{-1}
(y-\widehat\mu(\theta)\mathbf 1).
\]

The profile log-likelihood for \(\theta\), up to an additive constant, is

\[
\ell_p(\theta)
=
-\frac n2\log \widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
-\frac 12 \log |R_\theta|.
\]

Equivalently, we minimize

\[
n\log \widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)+\log |R_\theta|.
\]

The following code computes the MLEs.

```r
Xmat <- as.matrix(dat[, c("x1", "x2")])
yvec <- dat$y
n <- length(yvec)

D2 <- as.matrix(dist(Xmat))^2
one <- rep(1, n)

# small nugget only for numerical stability
nugget <- 1e-10

make_R <- function(theta) {
  exp(-theta * D2) + diag(nugget, n)
}

solve_chol <- function(U, b) {
  # R = t(U) %*% U
  backsolve(U, forwardsolve(t(U), b))
}

neg_prof_loglik <- function(logtheta) {
  theta <- exp(logtheta)
  R <- make_R(theta)
  
  U <- tryCatch(chol(R), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(U)) return(Inf)
  
  Rinv_one <- solve_chol(U, one)
  Rinv_y <- solve_chol(U, yvec)
  
  mu_hat <- as.numeric(crossprod(one, Rinv_y) /
                         crossprod(one, Rinv_one))
  
  resid <- yvec - mu_hat
  Rinv_resid <- solve_chol(U, resid)
  
  sigma2_hat <- as.numeric(crossprod(resid, Rinv_resid) / n)
  
  logdet_R <- 2 * sum(log(diag(U)))
  
  n * log(sigma2_hat) + logdet_R
}

opt <- optimize(
  neg_prof_loglik,
  interval = c(log(1e-6), log(1e3))
)

theta_hat <- exp(opt$minimum)

Rhat <- make_R(theta_hat)
Uhat <- chol(Rhat)

Rinv_one <- solve_chol(Uhat, one)
Rinv_y <- solve_chol(Uhat, yvec)

mu_hat <- as.numeric(crossprod(one, Rinv_y) /
                       crossprod(one, Rinv_one))

resid <- yvec - mu_hat
Rinv_resid <- solve_chol(Uhat, resid)

sigma2_hat <- as.numeric(crossprod(resid, Rinv_resid) / n)

cat("mu_hat     =", mu_hat, "\n")
cat("theta_hat  =", theta_hat, "\n")
cat("sigma2_hat =", sigma2_hat, "\n")
```

These are the MLEs for the simulated data.

---

# (3) BLUP and plug-in predictive distribution

For a new point \(x^\ast=(x_1^\ast,x_2^\ast)\), define

\[
r(x^\ast)
=
\left(
R_\theta(x^\ast,x_1),
\dots,
R_\theta(x^\ast,x_n)
\right)^\top.
\]

Using the fitted parameter values, the ordinary kriging BLUP is

\[
\widehat y(x^\ast)
=
\widehat\mu
+
r(x^\ast)^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
(y-\widehat\mu \mathbf 1).
\]

The plug-in predictive variance is

\[
\widehat s^2(x^\ast)
=
\widehat{\sigma}^2
\left[
1
-
r(x^\ast)^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1} r(x^\ast)
+
\frac{
\left\{
1-\mathbf 1^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1} r(x^\ast)
\right\}^2
}{
\mathbf 1^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}\mathbf 1
}
\right].
\]

Therefore the plug-in predictive distribution is

\[
Y(x^\ast)\mid y
\approx
N\left(
\widehat y(x^\ast),
\widehat s^2(x^\ast)
\right).
\]

The following prediction function implements this.

```r
alpha_hat <- solve_chol(Uhat, yvec - mu_hat * one)
denom_mu <- as.numeric(crossprod(one, Rinv_one))

gp_predict <- function(Xnew) {
  Xnew <- as.matrix(Xnew)
  if (ncol(Xnew) != 2) stop("Xnew must have two columns")
  
  out <- matrix(NA, nrow = nrow(Xnew), ncol = 2)
  colnames(out) <- c("mean", "se")
  
  for (k in 1:nrow(Xnew)) {
    x0 <- Xnew[k, ]
    
    d2 <- rowSums((Xmat - matrix(x0, nrow = n, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE))^2)
    r <- exp(-theta_hat * d2)
    
    Rinv_r <- solve_chol(Uhat, r)
    
    mean_k <- mu_hat + as.numeric(crossprod(r, alpha_hat))
    
    v1 <- as.numeric(crossprod(r, Rinv_r))
    v2 <- as.numeric(crossprod(one, Rinv_r))
    
    var_k <- sigma2_hat * (1 - v1 + (1 - v2)^2 / denom_mu)
    var_k <- max(var_k, 0)
    
    out[k, ] <- c(mean_k, sqrt(var_k))
  }
  
  as.data.frame(out)
}
```

---

# (4) BLUP and 95% predictive bands for the two slices

A 95% plug-in predictive interval is

\[
\widehat y(x^\ast)\pm 1.96\,\widehat s(x^\ast).
\]

## Slice \(x_2=2\)

```r
slice1 <- data.frame(x1 = xg, x2 = rep(2, length(xg)))
pred1 <- gp_predict(slice1)

upper1 <- pred1$mean + 1.96 * pred1$se
lower1 <- pred1$mean - 1.96 * pred1$se

plot(
  xg, goldstein(xg, 2),
  type = "l", lwd = 2,
  ylim = range(c(goldstein(xg, 2), lower1, upper1)),
  xlab = expression(x[1]),
  ylab = expression(y),
  main = expression(paste("GP BLUP with 95% bands: ", x[2] == 2))
)

polygon(
  c(xg, rev(xg)),
  c(upper1, rev(lower1)),
  col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.15),
  border = NA
)

lines(xg, goldstein(xg, 2), lwd = 2, col = "black")
lines(xg, pred1$mean, lwd = 2, col = "blue", lty = 2)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("True function", "GP BLUP", "95% predictive band"),
  col = c("black", "blue", rgb(0,0,1,0.15)),
  lty = c(1, 2, NA),
  lwd = c(2, 2, NA),
  pch = c(NA, NA, 15),
  bty = "n"
)
```

## Slice \(x_1=-2\)

```r
slice2 <- data.frame(x1 = rep(-2, length(xg)), x2 = xg)
pred2 <- gp_predict(slice2)

upper2 <- pred2$mean + 1.96 * pred2$se
lower2 <- pred2$mean - 1.96 * pred2$se

plot(
  xg, goldstein(-2, xg),
  type = "l", lwd = 2,
  ylim = range(c(goldstein(-2, xg), lower2, upper2)),
  xlab = expression(x[2]),
  ylab = expression(y),
  main = expression(paste("GP BLUP with 95% bands: ", x[1] == -2))
)

polygon(
  c(xg, rev(xg)),
  c(upper2, rev(lower2)),
  col = rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.15),
  border = NA
)

lines(xg, goldstein(-2, xg), lwd = 2, col = "black")
lines(xg, pred2$mean, lwd = 2, col = "red", lty = 2)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("True function", "GP BLUP", "95% predictive band"),
  col = c("black", "red", rgb(1,0,0,0.15)),
  lty = c(1, 2, NA),
  lwd = c(2, 2, NA),
  pch = c(NA, NA, 15),
  bty = "n"
)
```

---

# (5) Minimize the GP BLUP

We find

\[
\widehat x_{\text{GP}}
=
\arg\min_{x\in[-2,2]^2} \widehat y(x).
\]

Because the BLUP may be nonconvex, I use multistart box-constrained optimization.

```r
gp_mean <- function(z) {
  gp_predict(matrix(z, nrow = 1))$mean
}

set.seed(1)

starts <- rbind(
  c(0, -1),                                  # known plausible basin
  as.numeric(dat[which.min(dat$y), c("x1", "x2")]),
  matrix(runif(200 * 2, -2, 2), ncol = 2)
)

opt_list <- vector("list", nrow(starts))

for (i in 1:nrow(starts)) {
  opt_list[[i]] <- optim(
    par = starts[i, ],
    fn = gp_mean,
    method = "L-BFGS-B",
    lower = c(-2, -2),
    upper = c(2, 2)
  )
}

vals <- sapply(opt_list, function(o) o$value)
best <- which.min(vals)

xhat_gp <- opt_list[[best]]$par
yhat_gp <- opt_list[[best]]$value

cat("GP surrogate minimizer:\n")
cat("x1 =", xhat_gp[1], "\n")
cat("x2 =", xhat_gp[2], "\n")
cat("predicted y =", yhat_gp, "\n")
cat("true y at this point =", goldstein(xhat_gp[1], xhat_gp[2]), "\n")
```

The true Goldstein-Price minimizer is

\[
(0,-1),
\]

so a good surrogate should identify a point close to \((0,-1)\), although the exact GP surrogate minimizer depends on the 50-point training design.

---

# (6) Five additional training points

A principled choice is to add points using expected improvement, because the goal is optimization. Let

\[
f_{\min}=\min_{1\le i\le n} y_i
\]

be the current best observed value. For minimization, the improvement at \(x\) is

\[
I(x)=\max\{f_{\min}-Y(x),0\}.
\]

Under the plug-in Gaussian predictive distribution,

\[
Y(x)\mid y \approx N\{m(x),s^2(x)\},
\]

where \(m(x)=\widehat y(x)\) and \(s(x)=\widehat s(x)\). Define

\[
z(x)=\frac{f_{\min}-m(x)}{s(x)}.
\]

Then the expected improvement is

\[
\operatorname{EI}(x)
=
(f_{\min}-m(x))\Phi(z(x))
+
s(x)\phi(z(x)),
\]

where \(\Phi\) and \(\phi\) are the standard normal cdf and pdf. If \(s(x)=0\), define \(\operatorname{EI}(x)=0\).

The next point is

\[
x_{\text{new}}
=
\arg\max_{x\in[-2,2]^2} \operatorname{EI}(x).
\]

For five additional evaluations, I would choose points sequentially:

1. maximize EI using the current GP;
2. evaluate the deterministic simulator there;
3. refit the GP;
4. repeat until five points have been added.

This balances exploitation, by sampling near locations predicted to have low \(y\), and exploration, by sampling uncertain regions.

Implementation:

```r
EI <- function(z) {
  pr <- gp_predict(matrix(z, nrow = 1))
  m <- pr$mean
  s <- pr$se
  
  fmin <- min(yvec)
  
  if (s <= 1e-12) return(0)
  
  zz <- (fmin - m) / s
  
  ei <- (fmin - m) * pnorm(zz) + s * dnorm(zz)
  return(ei)
}

neg_EI <- function(z) -EI(z)

set.seed(2)

starts_EI <- rbind(
  xhat_gp,
  as.numeric(dat[which.min(dat$y), c("x1", "x2")]),
  matrix(runif(300 * 2, -2, 2), ncol = 2)
)

ei_opts <- vector("list", nrow(starts_EI))

for (i in 1:nrow(starts_EI)) {
  ei_opts[[i]] <- optim(
    par = starts_EI[i, ],
    fn = neg_EI,
    method = "L-BFGS-B",
    lower = c(-2, -2),
    upper = c(2, 2)
  )
}

ei_vals <- -sapply(ei_opts, function(o) o$value)
best_ei <- which.max(ei_vals)

x_next <- ei_opts[[best_ei]]$par
cat("First EI point:\n")
cat("x1 =", x_next[1], "\n")
cat("x2 =", x_next[2], "\n")
cat("EI =", ei_vals[best_ei], "\n")
```

For a complete sequential design of five points, wrap the GP fitting and EI optimization in a loop and refit after each new evaluation.

Conceptually, the five added settings should concentrate near the current estimated basin of the minimizer, usually near \((0,-1)\), while still including some points with large predictive uncertainty.

---

# (7) Spline-based surrogate and its minimizer

A natural spline-based model in two dimensions is a penalized thin-plate regression spline. The estimate solves

\[
\widehat f_\lambda
=
\arg\min_f
\left\{
\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-f(x_i))^2
+
\lambda J(f)
\right\},
\]

where, for a two-dimensional thin-plate spline,

\[
J(f)
=
\int\int
\left[
\left(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1^2}\right)^2
+
2\left(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1\partial x_2}\right)^2
+
\left(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_2^2}\right)^2
\right]
dx_1dx_2.
\]

The smoothing parameter \(\lambda\) can be selected by REML or GCV.

Because \(y\) is positive and varies greatly in magnitude, a log-response spline often behaves better. Since \(\log(\cdot)\) is monotone, minimizing the fitted log-response is equivalent to minimizing the fitted response on the transformed scale.

Using `mgcv`:

```r
library(mgcv)

dat$logy <- log(dat$y)

# Thin-plate spline on log(y)
spline_fit <- gam(
  logy ~ s(x1, x2, bs = "tp", k = 40),
  data = dat,
  method = "REML"
)

summary(spline_fit)
```

Define the spline predictor and minimize it over \([-2,2]^2\).

```r
spline_mean_log <- function(z) {
  predict(
    spline_fit,
    newdata = data.frame(x1 = z[1], x2 = z[2])
  )
}

set.seed(3)

starts_spline <- rbind(
  c(0, -1),
  as.numeric(dat[which.min(dat$y), c("x1", "x2")]),
  matrix(runif(200 * 2, -2, 2), ncol = 2)
)

spline_opts <- vector("list", nrow(starts_spline))

for (i in 1:nrow(starts_spline)) {
  spline_opts[[i]] <- optim(
    par = starts_spline[i, ],
    fn = spline_mean_log,
    method = "L-BFGS-B",
    lower = c(-2, -2),
    upper = c(2, 2)
  )
}

spline_vals <- sapply(spline_opts, function(o) o$value)
best_spline <- which.min(spline_vals)

xhat_spline <- spline_opts[[best_spline]]$par
logyhat_spline <- spline_opts[[best_spline]]$value
yhat_spline <- exp(logyhat_spline)

cat("Spline surrogate minimizer:\n")
cat("x1 =", xhat_spline[1], "\n")
cat("x2 =", xhat_spline[2], "\n")
cat("predicted y =", yhat_spline, "\n")
cat("true y at this point =", goldstein(xhat_spline[1], xhat_spline[2]), "\n")
```

If one wants a spline on the raw response instead, replace the model by

```r
spline_fit_raw <- gam(
  y ~ s(x1, x2, bs = "tp", k = 40),
  data = dat,
  method = "REML"
)
```

\[
x^\star_{\text{true}}=(0,-1).
\]

The GP and spline minimizers will not generally be identical because the GP interpolates smoothly according to the squared-exponential correlation, whereas the spline uses a penalized smoothness criterion.

## Preliminary reproducibility note

Parts (2), (5), (6), and (7) depend on the particular 50 simulated training points. Since the problem statement does not provide a random seed or the actual simulated data, there is no unique numerical value for the MLEs, the GP surrogate minimizer, the five added points, or the spline minimizer. Below I give a fully reproducible solution using a specified seed. Running the code produces the requested numerical estimates and plots.

I use an isotropic squared-exponential correlation

\[
\operatorname{Corr}\{Z(x),Z(x')\}
=
\exp\{-\theta \|x-x'\|^2\}.
\]

The true Goldstein-Price function has known global minimum

\[
x^\star_{\text{true}}=(0,-1),\qquad y(x^\star_{\text{true}})=3.
\]

---

# (1) Simulate \(n=50\) training points and visualize

Define the function and simulate training data.

```r
goldstein <- function(x1, x2) {
  A <- 1 + (x1 + x2 + 1)^2 *
    (19 - 14*x1 + 3*x1^2 - 14*x2 + 6*x1*x2 + 3*x2^2)
  
  B <- 30 + (2*x1 - 3*x2)^2 *
    (18 - 32*x1 + 12*x1^2 + 48*x2 - 36*x1*x2 + 27*x2^2)
  
  A * B
}

set.seed(2023)

n <- 50
X <- cbind(
  x1 = runif(n, -2, 2),
  x2 = runif(n, -2, 2)
)

y <- goldstein(X[,1], X[,2])

dat <- data.frame(x1 = X[,1], x2 = X[,2], y = y)
head(dat)
```

## (1a) True function versus \(x_1\) at \(x_2=2\)

```r
xg <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 500)

plot(
  xg, goldstein(xg, 2),
  type = "l", lwd = 2,
  xlab = expression(x[1]),
  ylab = expression(y(x[1], 2)),
  main = expression(paste("Goldstein-Price: ", x[2] == 2))
)
```

At \(x_2=2\), the function reduces to

\[
y(x_1,2)
=
\{1+(x_1+3)^2(3x_1^2-2x_1+3)\}
\{30+4(x_1-3)^2(12x_1^2-104x_1+222)\}.
\]

## (1b) True function versus \(x_2\) at \(x_1=-2\)

```r
plot(
  xg, goldstein(-2, xg),
  type = "l", lwd = 2,
  xlab = expression(x[2]),
  ylab = expression(y(-2, x[2])),
  main = expression(paste("Goldstein-Price: ", x[1] == -2))
)
```

At \(x_1=-2\), the function reduces to

\[
y(-2,x_2)
=
\{1+(x_2-1)^2(3x_2^2-26x_2+59)\}
\{30+(3x_2+4)^2(27x_2^2+120x_2+130)\}.
\]

## (1c) 3D plot with training data labelled

Because \(y\) varies over several orders of magnitude, I plot \(\log_{10}(y)\).

```r
library(plotly)

grid <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 80)
Z <- outer(grid, grid, function(a, b) goldstein(a, b))

plot_ly() %>%
  add_surface(
    x = grid,
    y = grid,
    z = log10(Z),
    opacity = 0.65,
    colorscale = "Viridis"
  ) %>%
  add_markers(
    x = dat$x1,
    y = dat$x2,
    z = log10(dat$y),
    text = paste0("point ", 1:n),
    marker = list(color = "red", size = 4)
  ) %>%
  layout(
    scene = list(
      xaxis = list(title = "x1"),
      yaxis = list(title = "x2"),
      zaxis = list(title = "log10(y)")
    ),
    title = "Goldstein-Price surface with 50 training points"
  )
```

---

# (2) GP surrogate and MLEs

We model

\[
Y(x)=\mu+Z(x),
\]

where

\[
Z(\cdot)\sim GP\{0,\sigma^2 R_\theta(\cdot,\cdot)\},
\]

with

\[
R_\theta(x,x')
=
\exp\{-\theta \|x-x'\|^2\}.
\]

Let

\[
R_\theta = \left[
\exp\{-\theta \|x_i-x_j\|^2\}
\right]_{i,j=1}^n.
\]

Then

\[
Y=(Y(x_1),\dots,Y(x_n))^\top
\sim
N_n(\mu \mathbf 1,\sigma^2 R_\theta).
\]

The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\mu,\sigma^2,\theta)
=
-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac n2\log \sigma^2
-\frac 12 \log |R_\theta|
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
(y-\mu \mathbf 1)^\top R_\theta^{-1}(y-\mu \mathbf 1).
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the MLE of \(\mu\) is the generalized least-squares estimator

\[
\widehat \mu(\theta)
=
\frac{\mathbf 1^\top R_\theta^{-1}y}
{\mathbf 1^\top R_\theta^{-1}\mathbf 1}.
\]

The MLE of \(\sigma^2\) is

\[
\widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
=
\frac{1}{n}
(y-\widehat\mu(\theta)\mathbf 1)^\top
R_\theta^{-1}
(y-\widehat\mu(\theta)\mathbf 1).
\]

The profile log-likelihood for \(\theta\), up to an additive constant, is

\[
\ell_p(\theta)
=
-\frac n2\log \widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
-\frac 12 \log |R_\theta|.
\]

Equivalently, we minimize

\[
n\log \widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)+\log |R_\theta|.
\]

The following code computes the MLEs.

```r
Xmat <- as.matrix(dat[, c("x1", "x2")])
yvec <- dat$y
n <- length(yvec)

D2 <- as.matrix(dist(Xmat))^2
one <- rep(1, n)

# small nugget only for numerical stability
nugget <- 1e-10

make_R <- function(theta) {
  exp(-theta * D2) + diag(nugget, n)
}

solve_chol <- function(U, b) {
  # R = t(U) %*% U
  backsolve(U, forwardsolve(t(U), b))
}

neg_prof_loglik <- function(logtheta) {
  theta <- exp(logtheta)
  R <- make_R(theta)
  
  U <- tryCatch(chol(R), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(U)) return(Inf)
  
  Rinv_one <- solve_chol(U, one)
  Rinv_y <- solve_chol(U, yvec)
  
  mu_hat <- as.numeric(crossprod(one, Rinv_y) /
                         crossprod(one, Rinv_one))
  
  resid <- yvec - mu_hat
  Rinv_resid <- solve_chol(U, resid)
  
  sigma2_hat <- as.numeric(crossprod(resid, Rinv_resid) / n)
  
  logdet_R <- 2 * sum(log(diag(U)))
  
  n * log(sigma2_hat) + logdet_R
}

opt <- optimize(
  neg_prof_loglik,
  interval = c(log(1e-6), log(1e3))
)

theta_hat <- exp(opt$minimum)

Rhat <- make_R(theta_hat)
Uhat <- chol(Rhat)

Rinv_one <- solve_chol(Uhat, one)
Rinv_y <- solve_chol(Uhat, yvec)

mu_hat <- as.numeric(crossprod(one, Rinv_y) /
                       crossprod(one, Rinv_one))

resid <- yvec - mu_hat
Rinv_resid <- solve_chol(Uhat, resid)

sigma2_hat <- as.numeric(crossprod(resid, Rinv_resid) / n)

cat("mu_hat     =", mu_hat, "\n")
cat("theta_hat  =", theta_hat, "\n")
cat("sigma2_hat =", sigma2_hat, "\n")
```

These are the MLEs for the simulated data.

---

# (3) BLUP and plug-in predictive distribution

For a new point \(x^\ast=(x_1^\ast,x_2^\ast)\), define

\[
r(x^\ast)
=
\left(
R_\theta(x^\ast,x_1),
\dots,
R_\theta(x^\ast,x_n)
\right)^\top.
\]

Using the fitted parameter values, the ordinary kriging BLUP is

\[
\widehat y(x^\ast)
=
\widehat\mu
+
r(x^\ast)^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
(y-\widehat\mu \mathbf 1).
\]

The plug-in predictive variance is

\[
\widehat s^2(x^\ast)
=
\widehat{\sigma}^2
\left[
1
-
r(x^\ast)^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1} r(x^\ast)
+
\frac{
\left\{
1-\mathbf 1^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1} r(x^\ast)
\right\}^2
}{
\mathbf 1^\top R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}\mathbf 1
}
\right].
\]

Therefore the plug-in predictive distribution is

\[
Y(x^\ast)\mid y
\approx
N\left(
\widehat y(x^\ast),
\widehat s^2(x^\ast)
\right).
\]

The following prediction function implements this.

```r
alpha_hat <- solve_chol(Uhat, yvec - mu_hat * one)
denom_mu <- as.numeric(crossprod(one, Rinv_one))

gp_predict <- function(Xnew) {
  Xnew <- as.matrix(Xnew)
  if (ncol(Xnew) != 2) stop("Xnew must have two columns")
  
  out <- matrix(NA, nrow = nrow(Xnew), ncol = 2)
  colnames(out) <- c("mean", "se")
  
  for (k in 1:nrow(Xnew)) {
    x0 <- Xnew[k, ]
    
    d2 <- rowSums((Xmat - matrix(x0, nrow = n, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE))^2)
    r <- exp(-theta_hat * d2)
    
    Rinv_r <- solve_chol(Uhat, r)
    
    mean_k <- mu_hat + as.numeric(crossprod(r, alpha_hat))
    
    v1 <- as.numeric(crossprod(r, Rinv_r))
    v2 <- as.numeric(crossprod(one, Rinv_r))
    
    var_k <- sigma2_hat * (1 - v1 + (1 - v2)^2 / denom_mu)
    var_k <- max(var_k, 0)
    
    out[k, ] <- c(mean_k, sqrt(var_k))
  }
  
  as.data.frame(out)
}
```

---

# (4) BLUP and 95% predictive bands for the two slices

A 95% plug-in predictive interval is

\[
\widehat y(x^\ast)\pm 1.96\,\widehat s(x^\ast).
\]

## Slice \(x_2=2\)

```r
slice1 <- data.frame(x1 = xg, x2 = rep(2, length(xg)))
pred1 <- gp_predict(slice1)

upper1 <- pred1$mean + 1.96 * pred1$se
lower1 <- pred1$mean - 1.96 * pred1$se

plot(
  xg, goldstein(xg, 2),
  type = "l", lwd = 2,
  ylim = range(c(goldstein(xg, 2), lower1, upper1)),
  xlab = expression(x[1]),
  ylab = expression(y),
  main = expression(paste("GP BLUP with 95% bands: ", x[2] == 2))
)

polygon(
  c(xg, rev(xg)),
  c(upper1, rev(lower1)),
  col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.15),
  border = NA
)

lines(xg, goldstein(xg, 2), lwd = 2, col = "black")
lines(xg, pred1$mean, lwd = 2, col = "blue", lty = 2)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("True function", "GP BLUP", "95% predictive band"),
  col = c("black", "blue", rgb(0,0,1,0.15)),
  lty = c(1, 2, NA),
  lwd = c(2, 2, NA),
  pch = c(NA, NA, 15),
  bty = "n"

```

## Slice \(x_1=-2\)

pred2 <- gp_predict(slice2)

upper2 <- pred2$mean + 1.96 * pred2$se
lower2 <- pred2$mean - 1.96 * pred2$se

  type = "l", lwd = 2,
  ylim = range(c(goldstein(-2, xg), lower2, upper2)),

  ylab = expression(y),
  main = expression(paste("GP BLUP with 95% bands: ", x[1] == -2))

  legend = c("True function", "GP BLUP", "95% predictive band"),
  col = c("black", "red", rgb(1,0,0,0.15)),
  lty = c(1, 2, NA),
  lwd = c(2, 2, NA),
  pch = c(NA, NA, 15),
  bty = "n"

---

# (5) Minimize the GP BLUP

We find

\[
\widehat x_{\text{GP}}
=
\arg\min_{x\in[-2,2]^2} \widehat y(x).
\]

Because the BLUP may be nonconvex, I use multistart box-constrained optimization.

```r
gp_mean <- function(z) {
  gp_predict(matrix(z, nrow = 1))$mean
}

set.seed(1)

starts <- rbind(
  c(0, -1),                                  # known plausible basin
  as.numeric(dat[which.min(dat$y), c("x1", "x2")]),
  matrix(runif(200 * 2, -2, 2), ncol = 2)
)

opt_list <- vector("list", nrow(starts))

for (i in 1:nrow(starts)) {
  opt_list[[i]] <- optim(
    par = starts[i, ],
    fn = gp_mean,
    method = "L-BFGS-B",
    lower = c(-2, -2),
    upper = c(2, 2)
  )
}

vals <- sapply(opt_list, function(o) o$value)
best <- which.min(vals)

xhat_gp <- opt_list[[best]]$par
yhat_gp <- opt_list[[best]]$value

cat("GP surrogate minimizer:\n")
cat("x1 =", xhat_gp[1], "\n")
cat("x2 =", xhat_gp[2], "\n")
cat("predicted y =", yhat_gp, "\n")
cat("true y at this point =", goldstein(xhat_gp[1], xhat_gp[2]), "\n")
```

The true Goldstein-Price minimizer is

\[
(0,-1),
\]

so a good surrogate should identify a point close to \((0,-1)\), although the exact GP surrogate minimizer depends on the 50-point training design.

---

# (6) Five additional training points

A principled choice is to add points using expected improvement, because the goal is optimization. Let

\[
f_{\min}=\min_{1\le i\le n} y_i
\]

be the current best observed value. For minimization, the improvement at \(x\) is

\[
I(x)=\max\{f_{\min}-Y(x),0\}.
\]

Under the plug-in Gaussian predictive distribution,

\[
Y(x)\mid y \approx N\{m(x),s^2(x)\},
\]

where \(m(x)=\widehat y(x)\) and \(s(x)=\widehat s(x)\). Define

\[
z(x)=\frac{f_{\min}-m(x)}{s(x)}.
\]

Then the expected improvement is

\[
\operatorname{EI}(x)
=
(f_{\min}-m(x))\Phi(z(x))
+
s(x)\phi(z(x)),
\]

where \(\Phi\) and \(\phi\) are the standard normal cdf and pdf. If \(s(x)=0\), define \(\operatorname{EI}(x)=0\).

The next point is

\[
x_{\text{new}}
=
\arg\max_{x\in[-2,2]^2} \operatorname{EI}(x).
\]

For five additional evaluations, I would choose points sequentially:

1. maximize EI using the current GP;
2. evaluate the deterministic simulator there;
3. refit the GP;
4. repeat until five points have been added.

This balances exploitation, by sampling near locations predicted to have low \(y\), and exploration, by sampling uncertain regions.

Implementation:

```r
EI <- function(z) {
  pr <- gp_predict(matrix(z, nrow = 1))
  m <- pr$mean
  s <- pr$se
  
  fmin <- min(yvec)
  
  if (s <= 1e-12) return(0)
  
  zz <- (fmin - m) / s
  
  ei <- (fmin - m) * pnorm(zz) + s * dnorm(zz)
  return(ei)
}

neg_EI <- function(z) -EI(z)

set.seed(2)

starts_EI <- rbind(
  xhat_gp,
  as.numeric(dat[which.min(dat$y), c("x1", "x2")]),
  matrix(runif(300 * 2, -2, 2), ncol = 2)
)

ei_opts <- vector("list", nrow(starts_EI))

for (i in 1:nrow(starts_EI)) {
  ei_opts[[i]] <- optim(
    par = starts_EI[i, ],
    fn = neg_EI,
    method = "L-BFGS-B",
    lower = c(-2, -2),
    upper = c(2, 2)
  )
}

ei_vals <- -sapply(ei_opts, function(o) o$value)
best_ei <- which.max(ei_vals)

x_next <- ei_opts[[best_ei]]$par
cat("First EI point:\n")
cat("x1 =", x_next[1], "\n")
cat("x2 =", x_next[2], "\n")
cat("EI =", ei_vals[best_ei], "\n")
```

For a complete sequential design of five points, wrap the GP fitting and EI optimization in a loop and refit after each new evaluation.

Conceptually, the five added settings should concentrate near the current estimated basin of the minimizer, usually near \((0,-1)\), while still including some points with large predictive uncertainty.

---

# (7) Spline-based surrogate and its minimizer

A natural spline-based model in two dimensions is a penalized thin-plate regression spline. The estimate solves

\[
\widehat f_\lambda
=
\arg\min_f
\left\{
\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-f(x_i))^2
+
\lambda J(f)
\right\},
\]

where, for a two-dimensional thin-plate spline,

\[
J(f)
=
\int\int
\left[
\left(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1^2}\right)^2
+
2\left(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_1\partial x_2}\right)^2
+
\left(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_2^2}\right)^2
\right]
dx_1dx_2.
\]

The smoothing parameter \(\lambda\) can be selected by REML or GCV.

Because \(y\) is positive and varies greatly in magnitude, a log-response spline often behaves better. Since \(\log(\cdot)\) is monotone, minimizing the fitted log-response is equivalent to minimizing the fitted response on the transformed scale.

Using `mgcv`:

```r
library(mgcv)

dat$logy <- log(dat$y)

# Thin-plate spline on log(y)
spline_fit <- gam(
  logy ~ s(x1, x2, bs = "tp", k = 40),
  data = dat,
  method = "REML"
)

summary(spline_fit)
```

Define the spline predictor and minimize it over \([-2,2]^2\).

```r
spline_mean_log <- function(z) {
  predict(
    spline_fit,
    newdata = data.frame(x1 = z[1], x2 = z[2])
  )
}

set.seed(3)

starts_spline <- rbind(
  c(0, -1),
  as.numeric(dat[which.min(dat$y), c("x1", "x2")]),
  matrix(runif(200 * 2, -2, 2), ncol = 2)
)

spline_opts <- vector("list", nrow(starts_spline))

for (i in 1:nrow(starts_spline)) {
  spline_opts[[i]] <- optim(
    par = starts_spline[i, ],
    fn = spline_mean_log,
    method = "L-BFGS-B",
    lower = c(-2, -2),
    upper = c(2, 2)
  )
}

spline_vals <- sapply(spline_opts, function(o) o$value)
best_spline <- which.min(spline_vals)

xhat_spline <- spline_opts[[best_spline]]$par
logyhat_spline <- spline_opts[[best_spline]]$value
yhat_spline <- exp(logyhat_spline)

cat("Spline surrogate minimizer:\n")
cat("x1 =", xhat_spline[1], "\n")
cat("x2 =", xhat_spline[2], "\n")
cat("predicted y =", yhat_spline, "\n")
cat("true y at this point =", goldstein(xhat_spline[1], xhat_spline[2]), "\n")
```

If one wants a spline on the raw response instead, replace the model by

```r
spline_fit_raw <- gam(
  y ~ s(x1, x2, bs = "tp", k = 40),
  data = dat,
  method = "REML"
)
```

and then minimize its predicted value in the same way.

A well-fitting spline surrogate should again give a minimizer near the true value

\[
x^\star_{\text{true}}=(0,-1).
\]

The GP and spline minimizers will not generally be identical because the GP interpolates smoothly according to the squared-exponential correlation, whereas the spline uses a penalized smoothness criterion.
